title: Least Health to Cross the Vault
statement:
A courier enters a vault laid out as a grid vault with m rows and n columns. They start in the top-left room and must reach the bottom-right room, moving only right or down one room at a time.

Every room changes the courier's health by vault[i][j]: a negative value is a trap that removes health, a positive value is a medkit that adds it, and 0 does nothing. This includes the first and the last room.

The courier starts with some whole number of health points. If their health ever drops to 0 or below, even for a moment, they fail. Return the smallest starting health that lets them reach the exit along some path.

examples.why: Going right first: 4 − 3 = 1, then 5, then 3. Going down first would need 12. The first room alone already forces at least 4.
Right, right, down ends with the most health, but the −5 early on needs 6 to start. Down, right, right loses 3 in small steps and only needs 4.
No damage anywhere, but the courier must start alive, so the answer is never below 1.

hints: Walking forward, you have to track two things at once: current health and the lowest point so far. Try walking backward from the exit instead.
Ask: to stand in room (i, j) and still finish, how much health do I need on entering it? The exit room only depends on its own value.
need[i][j] = max(1, min(need of the room to the right, need of the room below) − vault[i][j]). The max with 1 is what stops a big medkit from 'pre-paying' damage you have not taken yet.

explain.intuition:
The forward direction is awkward. A path that ends with lots of health can still dip to zero early, so "best health so far" does not tell you which path is safest. You would need to carry both the current health and the worst dip, and those two pull in different directions.

Backward it becomes one number. Let need[i][j] be the health you must have on entering room (i, j) to finish. From there you go right or down, so you pick the cheaper of the two neighbours, then account for this room: need − vault[i][j]. If this room is a big medkit the result might be 0 or negative, but you still have to be alive when you walk in, so clamp it to at least 1. That clamp is the whole trick: health gained later cannot pay for damage taken earlier.
steps: Fill a table from the bottom-right corner back to the top-left.
For the exit room: need = max(1, 1 − vault[m−1][n−1]).
For every other room, take the smaller need of the room to the right and the room below (only the ones inside the grid).
Return need[0][0]. One row of the table is enough if you want O(n) memory.
pitfalls: Running the DP forward and picking the path with the highest total. In the second example that path needs more health, because its big loss comes first.
Forgetting the max(1, …) clamp. Without it a medkit near the end lowers the answer below what the start of the path actually needs.
Ignoring the first or last room. Both change health too, as in the first example where the starting trap alone sets the answer.

solutions.title: Binary search on the starting health
solutions.idea: For a fixed start, a forward DP keeps the most health you can have in each room while staying alive. More starting health never hurts, so binary search the smallest start that reaches the exit.

solutions.title: Backward DP on the health needed
solutions.idea: need[i][j] is the health required on entering room (i, j). Fill it from the exit back to the start, clamping to at least 1.

followups: Return the actual path, not just the health. What do you store?
The courier may also move left. Why does the simple table no longer work, and what would you use instead?
